effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative study; reports descriptive user-fee and connection-fee figures mentioned by interviewees rather than statistical effect estimates.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Container-based sanitation (CBS, e.g., Fresh Life Toilets) was perceived positively as a safe, reliable, space-saving sanitation option in Mukuru Kwa Reuben where lack of land ownership, limited space, and lack of clear utility mandates impede conventional sewerage and pit latrines; however, scaling and equitable access were constrained by absent regulatory standards for off-grid sanitation, fragmented ministerial mandates and uncoordinated infrastructure projects (e.g., road expansions demolishing CBS toilets without consultation), unmet land tenure and title-deed bureaucracies, informal cartels controlling access and pricing, lack of community consultation, and public underfunding shifting regressive user fees onto residents (reported at 850 KES/month for Fresh Life toilets, 3–5 KES per use for public toilets, 1,000–2,000 KES/month in household sanitation spending, and a 5,000 KES connection fee for simplified sewer projects).
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF p. 1, Abstract; PDF pp. 5–8, Sections 3.1–3.3.2; Table 1, PDF p. 5

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative study (capped at ceiling 2) that directly documents through interviews with government officials, a local chief, landlords, and residents how institutional fragmentation, lack of utility service mandates and off-grid standards, insecure tenure/title-deed bureaucracy, uncoordinated demolitions, lack of consultation, and user/connection fees constrain sanitation access.

evidence_quotes.quote: Twenty-five (25) participants comprising 10 community members, 10 landlords/ structure owners (availability in the informal settlements), one local chief and four ministry officials working the sanitation sector were sampled for participation.
Government utilities underprovided the sanitation services, partly because they do not have a clear obligation to serve informal settlements and because of the fluid and rapidly urbanizing cities.

Others include bureaucracies of acquiring title deeds, and sometimes cultural norms which disassociate people from their responsibility of ensuring safe excreta management. Unmet land tenure in the informal settlements affected sanitation innovations in informal settlements.

Beyond the financial issues, there was an observed deficit in grassroots engagement, characterized by inadequate community involvement and consultations. This lack of community-level participation and buy-in undermined the long-term adoption and maintenance of sanitation facilities, suggesting that solutions were often imposed rather than collaboratively developed.
The sanitation docket is like an orphaned child; Roles and responsibilities are fragmented between various Ministries like Water and Sanitation (focuses more on water provision) and Health (hygiene).
Consequently, access depended heavily on a user-fee model, creating an economic barrier.
